newsitem.title: USA: POLL--Wall Street experts see no Fed move in July.
newsitem.headline: POLL--Wall Street experts see no Fed move in July.

text.p: Economists in a Reuters poll were unanimous in predicting no change in interest rates at the Federal Reserve's two-day montarey policy meeting July 1-2.
All 36 analysts polled on Monday said the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) would keep the federal funds rate steady at 5.50 percent.
The last time an overwhelming number of Wall Street experts agreed on "no move" in monetary policy was before the December 17, 1996, FOMC meeting.

Looking forward to the August 19 FOMC meeting, 16 of the 36 poll respondents said the Fed would keep policy unchanged, 15 said policymakers would vote to boost interest rates by 25 basis points, and the rest said they were uncertain.
Despite recent evidence of slower U.S. economic growth, the economy has clearly benefitted from a strong labor market and appears near full capacity levels.
However, analysts said that without an inflation threat, FOMC members would have a difficult time justifying a rate hike to the American public.
"If the Fed moves without inflation, then Congress and a lot of other people will come down on them," said Scott Pardee, senior economic adviser at Yamaichi International America Inc.
The Fed faced harsh bipartisan criticism from Congress after it decided to raise rates in March.
Pardee, who sees just a 10 percent chance of a rate rise this week, said that as long as inflation is not a threat, "there is no compelling reason for the Fed to move."
Currently, the economy contains some scattered signs of inflationary pressures, but rising prices in most consumer goods and services have yet to surface.
In addition, there are few wage pressures despite the fact that the 4.8-percent May unemployment rate is the lowest level since October 1973 when it hit 4.6 percent.

John Williams, chief global economist at Bankers Trust Co, said there are temporary factors holding the inflation beast down, such as worker anxiety, declining healthcare costs and a strong dollar. But those forces are not going to last forever, he said.
"There are lags, and you have to give the lags a chance to work through," said Williams, who leans toward a rate hike at the FOMC meeting on August 19.
The economists who forecast more tightening in months to come said the current trend of slowing growth and consumer spending is bound to reverse itself.
Consumer confidence as measured by the Conference Board jumped to 129.6 in June, the highest level since August 1969.

Many experts read the confidence report as a sign that consumer spending -- the driving force behind the 5.9-percent gross domestic product growth rate in the first quarter of 1997 -- should trend upward again in the forseeable future.
"The underlying consumer sentiment is strong and that will (show up) in data by the FOMC meeting in August," said David Sloan, senior economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A.
